system: You are an expert reviewer of machine-learning research ideas.
user:
Compare two research ideas for the SAME research problem and pick the stronger one.

Research problem: In MVFA's few-shot inference, the released code min-max normalises the zero-shot (text) branch and the few-shot (memory-bank) branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set and adds them with a fixed weight of 0.5, so the score of one image depends on the rest of the test set and a single incoming image cannot be scored. Can this transductive normalisation be replaced by an inductive one computed only from the K normal support images, at a small cost in AUROC? The inductive normaliser maps each branch's patch scores through the 1st and 99th percentiles of the leave-one-out patch scores of the supports (every patch of support i scored against the memory bank of the other K-1 supports and against the text anchors), which gives thousands of reference values even at K = 2; the fusion weight and the max pooling of the image score are kept fixed. Primary outcome: image-level and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive normalisation on each held-out BMAD dataset for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the original method's AUROC across random half-size test subsets and at shifted prevalence (10% and 50% abnormal). Secondary outcome: sensitivity at 95% specificity with a threshold fixed from the support scores alone.

A stronger idea is one whose proposed change acts on the SPECIFIC mechanism of the target method that causes the problem (here: the released MVFA code and its verified behaviour), rather than a generic improvement that would apply to any anomaly detector.

Judge on:
1. Specificity. Would this idea plausibly solve THIS problem in THIS method better than a generic alternative? A mechanism that applies equally to any model and any problem is WEAKER, not stronger, because it does not explain why it fixes this problem.
2. Evidence. Is the proposed mechanism supported by the cited literature or by verified properties of the code and the benchmark?
3. Testability. Does the idea make a concrete, falsifiable prediction that can be checked on BMAD with one Colab GPU?

Explicitly DO NOT reward: length or polish of the write-up, stacking many modules, vague "add an attention/adapter module" proposals, or ideas that need data, labels or compute that are not available.

Idea A:
TITLE: Self-referenced residuals: removing each image's own score offset before support-CDF mapping
SUMMARY: Subtract from every patch score the median of the same image's own patch scores (a per-image offset reflecting acquisition and intensity) and map the residual through the leave-one-out support CDF of residuals computed the same way, which stays strictly inductive because it uses only the image itself and the supports.
HYPOTHESIS: Self-referenced residual normalisation improves image AUROC by at least 1.5 points over the exact leave-one-out residual CDF on held-out datasets with strong acquisition variation (ChestXray, HIS, OCT17), and changes it by less than 0.5 points on the others.
RATIONALE: The residual-CDF parents remove offsets that depend on position, but much of the variation in medical scores is per image: scanner, intensity window, stain, patient size. An image's own median patch score measures this offset without any other test image, because most of every image — even an abnormal one — is normal tissue. Subtracting it before mapping through a reference built the same way from supports removes per-image offsets inductively; diffuse lesions that shift the median are the risk, which the per-dataset evaluation measures.
METHOD: 1) test_few.py: for every image (supports and tests) and each branch and level: r_j = s_j - median(s); for supports use leave-one-out bank scores. 2) Reference R = pooled support residuals; F(r) by searchsorted. 3) 0.5 fusion and max pooling unchanged; test-set min-max removed. 4) Ablation: positional + self-referenced residual. No training.
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together), MVFA retrained with source-validation selection; K in {2, 4, 8, 16}; 3 seeds x 3 support draws; 0.5 fusion and max pooling unchanged. Baselines: transductive MVFA pipeline, support percentiles (problem statement). Additional baselines: exact LOO residual CDF; global CDF. Diagnostic: correlation of per-image median score with image AUROC loss. Falsified if no gain on ChestXray, HIS or OCT17.

Idea B:
TITLE: Augmented-support reference sets for inductive normalisation at small K
SUMMARY: Enlarge the leave-one-out reference set of every normaliser by scoring label-preserving augmentations of the K normal supports (flips, small shifts and rotations, mild intensity jitter), so the reference distribution reflects normal variability even at K = 2.
HYPOTHESIS: At K = 2, building the empirical-CDF reference from 16 augmentations per support reduces the standard deviation of image AUROC across support draws by at least 30% and increases mean pixel AUROC by at least 1 point over the unaugmented reference, with no benefit expected at K = 16.
RATIONALE: Both parents spend all their effort on how to map scores, while their common weakness is how few normal scores are available: at K = 2 the reference consists of two images scored against a one-image bank. A different lever is the reference itself. Normal anatomy varies by position, orientation and intensity; label-preserving augmentations of the supports sample this variation and give many more leave-one-out reference scores without any extra data. Augmented views are scored against the bank of the other supports only, so the scheme stays strictly inductive.
METHOD: 1) utils.py: augment(x, n=16): horizontal flip (where anatomically valid), shifts up to 8 px, rotations up to 10 degrees, gamma in [0.8, 1.2]. 2) build_refs: for each support i and each augmented view, few-shot scores against the bank of the other supports (unaugmented) and zero-shot scores; pool into the reference arrays. 3) test_few.py: empirical CDF per branch and level; 0.5 fusion and max pooling unchanged; test-set min-max removed. Hyper-parameters: n in {4, 16, 64}. No training.
EXPERIMENT: Leave-one-modality-out on BMAD (RESC and OCT17 held out together), MVFA retrained with source-validation selection; K in {2, 4, 8, 16}; 3 seeds x 3 support draws; 0.5 fusion and max pooling unchanged. Baselines: transductive MVFA pipeline, support percentiles (problem statement). Additional baseline: unaugmented empirical CDF. Metrics: mean and standard deviation of image/pixel AUROC across support draws per K. Falsified if variance at K = 2 is not reduced by 30%.

Respond in exactly this format:
REASONING: <one to three sentences explaining your choice>
CONFIDENCE: <HIGH | MEDIUM | LOW>
WINNER=<A | B | TIE>
response:
REASONING: Idea A directly tackles the primary failure mode of inductive normalisation in MVFA across medical modalities—large per-image score shifts driven by scanner/intensity variations that transductive min-maxing previously absorbed across the test set. In contrast, Idea B simply uses standard data augmentations to increase sample count, which is weakly motivated given the baseline already yields thousands of patch-level scores even at K=2.
CONFIDENCE: HIGH
WINNER=A
